sources.title: Using approved third-party equipment with Xfinity Internet and Xfinity Voice
sources.evidenceNote: Customer-owned modems, routers, and gateways are allowed when certified and suitable for the member's service; model, speed-tier, address, and Voice compatibility require Xfinity's current device check.

sources.title: Device Info — Xfinity Compatible Modems
sources.evidenceNote: Xfinity's address- and plan-aware database is the final check for current modem recommendations and compatibility.

sources.title: Learn About AT&T Internet Equipment
sources.evidenceNote: AT&T provides the Wi-Fi gateway that connects AT&T Internet or Fiber service to the home.

sources.title: Get Help With DMZ+ Zone Devices
sources.evidenceNote: AT&T documents IP Passthrough for BGW210 and BGW320 gateways, allowing one downstream device to receive the passthrough assignment.

sources.title: Connect your Devices to T-Mobile Internet
sources.evidenceNote: Third-party routers connect to the T-Mobile gateway by Ethernet; supported Wi-Fi 6 mesh/extender products are compatible; the T-Mobile gateway does not offer bridge mode.

sources.title: Authorized Modems to Use on the Spectrum Network
sources.evidenceNote: Spectrum maintains the current authorized-modem list; exact eligibility remains model-, service-, and location-dependent and must be rechecked before purchase or activation.

sources.title: Advanced Wireless Gateway — Spectrum Community
sources.evidenceNote: A verified Spectrum employee states that Spectrum supplies separate modem and router equipment and that a customer router can connect directly to the modem.

sources.title: Using Your Own Modem Device With Cox Internet
sources.evidenceNote: Cox permits customer-owned equipment when the exact modem is certified for the network and selected tier; a separate router is needed when the modem does not include routing or Wi-Fi.

sources.title: Cox Certified Cable Modems
sources.evidenceNote: Cox's current device list is the final model and speed-tier check; unsupported devices are not activated as new or replacement equipment.

sources.title: MoCA to Ethernet Self Install for Fios Internet Speed Upgrade
sources.evidenceNote: Verizon identifies the ONT as the device that converts the fiber signal into separate TV, voice, and data signals and documents the Ethernet handoff used for upgraded internet service.

sources.title: Self-Install Verizon Fios Services
sources.evidenceNote: Fios service depends on an installed ONT whose status and eligibility are verified by Verizon; router setup occurs downstream of that optical termination.

sources.title: Fios Customer Agreement
sources.evidenceNote: The current agreement recognizes routers or extenders purchased from Verizon or a third party and states that Verizon set-top-box streaming requires a compatible Fios router.

sources.title: Fios TV Home App FAQs
sources.evidenceNote: Verizon documents that non-Verizon routers cannot access every Fios TV Home app function and that some multi-router arrangements can block streaming or automatic pairing.

sources.title: What Are Multi-Gig Ethernet and 2.5G Multi-Gig Ethernet Ports?
sources.evidenceNote: NETGEAR documents 1, 2.5, and 5 Gbps multi-gig rates and explains that a gigabit port limits a multi-gig connection to a 1 Gbps Ethernet line rate.

sources.title: IEEE 802.3 2.5G/5GBASE-T (NGEABT) Task Force Objectives
sources.evidenceNote: Approved objectives define 2.5 Gb/s operation up to at least 100 m on four-pair Class D (Cat5e) cabling, 5 Gb/s up to at least 100 m on Class E (Cat6), and 5 Gb/s up to 100 m on Class D only for defined use cases and deployment configurations. Auto-Negotiation (Clause 28) support is an objective.

sources.title: IEEE P802.3an 10GBASE-T Task Force Objectives
sources.evidenceNote: Approved objectives define 10 Gb/s operation over at least 100 m of four-pair Class F cabling and at least 55 m to 100 m of four-pair Class E (Cat6) cabling, which is why a Cat6 run is a distance-limited 10G path rather than a guaranteed one.

sources.title: What is the difference between router mode and AP mode?
sources.evidenceNote: Access-point mode disables router features including the guest network, site blocking, VPN service, and remote management. NETGEAR recommends bridging the ISP gateway and keeping the retail router in router mode; AP mode with gateway Wi-Fi disabled is the fallback when bridge mode is unavailable.

sources.title: How do I fix problems caused by my NETGEAR Orbi or Nighthawk router connected to an ISP gateway?
sources.evidenceNote: A retail router behind an ISP gateway performs double network address translation. The documented fixes are putting the ISP gateway in bridge mode, or turning off the gateway's Wi-Fi and putting the retail router in access-point mode.

sources.title: Use Bridge Mode on your wireless gateway
sources.evidenceNote: Xfinity publishes a bridge-mode procedure for using a customer-owned router in combination with an Xfinity Wireless Gateway.

sources.title: Are all eeros the same?
sources.evidenceNote: eero states that its current models are compatible with previously supported eero models, and that combining newer units with older-generation units on the same network may reduce performance across the network.

sources.title: eero Max 7
sources.evidenceNote: eero confirms a current-generation unit can be used with existing eeros, while recommending same-generation devices across the network for optimal performance.

sources.title: RBS760 — Orbi 760 Series Tri-band WiFi 6 Mesh Add-on Satellite
sources.evidenceNote: NETGEAR lists the matching series router (RBR760) as a system requirement for this add-on satellite and describes it as adding coverage to an Orbi 760 Series system, which is why Orbi pairing is treated as a per-series question.

sources.title: Mix and Match Deco Models — Deco Compatibility Guide
sources.evidenceNote: TP-Link states that different Deco models can be combined in one mesh network, that the main Deco determines which features are available network-wide, and that a feature works only when every unit supports it.

sources.title: TP-Link Mesh Compatibility: Deco, OneMesh, EasyMesh and Omada
sources.evidenceNote: TP-Link states that its Deco, Archer OneMesh/EasyMesh, and Omada lines cannot interoperate in a single unified mesh network and that seamless roaming between them is not supported.

sources.title: What is AiMesh and AiMesh Router
sources.evidenceNote: ASUS states that AiMesh connects multiple compatible ASUS routers, lets different AiMesh-compatible models be mixed, and gives every device in the network access to the main router's features.

sources.title: Nest Wifi Pro mesh compatibility
sources.evidenceNote: Google states that Nest Wifi Pro is not backwards compatible and cannot be combined with earlier Nest Wifi or Google Wifi routers or points in a single mesh network, because those models cannot support the 6 GHz band Nest Wifi Pro meshes over.

sources.title: Use Nest Wifi and Google Wifi devices on the same network
sources.evidenceNote: Google states that Nest Wifi and Google Wifi devices can be combined on one network, that a Nest Wifi point must be added after a router or Google Wifi point exists, and that Nest Wifi Pro is excluded from those combinations.

sources.title: Alternative Topologies — Wi-Fi EasyMesh
sources.evidenceNote: The Wi-Fi Alliance describes Wi-Fi EasyMesh as a standards-based multi-AP approach whose listed capabilities include scalability by enabling the addition of Wi-Fi EasyMesh access points from multiple vendors.

sources.title: Wi-Fi CERTIFIED Product Finder
sources.evidenceNote: The Wi-Fi Alliance publishes a searchable database of Wi-Fi CERTIFIED products, which is the authoritative way to confirm whether a specific model carries a certification such as Wi-Fi EasyMesh rather than only using the word mesh in marketing.

sources.title: Wi-Fi (MAC/PHY) — Generational Wi-Fi
sources.evidenceNote: The Wi-Fi Alliance dates Wi-Fi 4 to 2009, Wi-Fi 5 to 2014, Wi-Fi 6 to 2018, and Wi-Fi 7 to 2024; it states Wi-Fi 7 enhances performance in the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz bands, that Wi-Fi 6E certification extends Wi-Fi 6 to the 6 GHz band, and that 320 MHz channels are available in the 6 GHz band.

sources.title: Faster and more secure Wi-Fi in Windows
sources.evidenceNote: Microsoft states that Wi-Fi 7 is available starting with Windows 11 version 24H2, that a supporting router and adapter are both required, that `netsh wlan show drivers` reports supported radio types such as 802.11be and 802.11ax plus WPA3 support, and that roaming between a WPA2 and a WPA3 access point requires an adapter supporting cross-roaming.

sources.title: How to Enable 6 GHz Band Using Intel Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 Products
sources.evidenceNote: Intel lists the 6 GHz prerequisites as Windows 11 with current updates, driver 22.70.0 or later for Wi-Fi 6E and 23.10.0 or later for Wi-Fi 7, a compatible 6E or 7 router, and Windows 11 24H2 for Wi-Fi 7 functionality; it also notes that some countries prohibit the 6 GHz band and that a system manufacturer may not have enabled it.

sources.title: USB 3.2
sources.evidenceNote: USB-IF states that the USB 3.2 specification identifies three transfer rates — 20 Gbps, 10 Gbps, and 5 Gbps — and that products are backwards compatible with all existing USB products and will operate at the lowest common speed capability.

sources.title: USB Interface Standards and Theoretical Speeds
sources.evidenceNote: Western Digital's table lists USB 2.0 (Hi-Speed USB) at a 480 Mbps theoretical maximum with 240 Mbps typical real-world speed, and USB 3.2 Gen 1 at 5 Gbps theoretical with 3.2 Gbps typical, noting that real-world speed varies by connection, operating system, and file mix.

sources.title: USB31000S — USB 3.0 to Gigabit Ethernet Network Adapter datasheet
sources.evidenceNote: StarTech states that its USB 3.0 gigabit adapter supports gigabit connections at full bandwidth unlike USB 2.0 adapters, that it remains backward compatible with USB 2.0/1.x systems with speed limited by the USB bus, and that USB 2.0 adapters cannot provide true gigabit speeds.
